# Player values are not additive: 89 synergies, 61 anti-synergies, and a five-win fit claim

**What it is** — The speaker, Ben Jenkins, measures synergy by comparing how pairs perform together on the court versus off it, shown in a two-way quadrant plot: upper right is two-way synergy (better on offense and defense together), lower left is two-way anti-synergy (worse on both) (JjeFktc4QLM [09:40], [10:10]). He reports 89 positive synergies and 61 anti-synergies (JjeFktc4QLM [10:10]). He argues traditional metrics assume additivity: two players each at plus two per 100 possessions are assumed to give plus four, which "doesn't actually happen in reality" (JjeFktc4QLM [10:10], [10:41]). Adding synergy explains some of the "win residual" (actual results minus the model's prediction) (JjeFktc4QLM [11:11]). His headline: "two equally talented rosters can differ five plus wins solely based on their fit" (JjeFktc4QLM [11:11], [12:43]). For Rudy Gobert-type defenders he says a team of scorers around them matters, and that defensive specialists are undervalued by traditional metrics, which he calls a potential competitive advantage (JjeFktc4QLM [09:40]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's explanation is complementarity: spacing, screens and rotations make one player's value depend on teammates, and deterrence on defense does not show up in box scores (JjeFktc4QLM [05:38]). The five-win figure is reported without how it was computed (JjeFktc4QLM [11:11]).

**When to apply** — As a prompt to check whether a unit's results differ from the sum of its parts. Inference: for the offensive line, compare five-man combinations that played together against a simple sum of per-player PFF grades. When PFF defensive grades and counting stats disagree for a player, treat the gap as a question for film, not a tie-break (Inference). Eric's baseline: no direct position on synergy or player-fit models (method-baseline.md).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: all figures are from NBA data with no uncertainty shown, and the 89 and 61 counts carry no definition of a threshold in the captions. A judge's portability objection to Shapley values (see [[framework--neural-shapley-credit-and-player-dropout]]) applies directly, and pairs who almost always play together give few samples (JjeFktc4QLM [16:21]). The "market inefficiency" and trade-fit claims are the author's view (JjeFktc4QLM [09:40], [10:41]). College rosters turn over yearly and units are larger, so NBA pair results do not transfer to line continuity without checking (Inference).

**Example** — The speaker's additivity example: two players at plus two points per 100 possessions assumed to sum to plus four (JjeFktc4QLM [10:10]).

# Case study: Rudy Gobert ranks 54th on traditional metrics and 12th on the model

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins decomposes player value by source. Nikola Jokic ranks first in the top 15 and excels at playmaking, scoring and defensive rebounding; Stephen Curry scores very well and is weaker on defense; Rudy Gobert's value is "largely defensive presence and defensive actions" (JjeFktc4QLM [08:09], [08:40], [09:10]). The speaker says Gobert is traditionally ranked 54th, the model has him 12th, and "the box score missed 45% of his defensive value", which he links to opponents scoring less and getting fewer paint opportunities when Gobert is on the floor (JjeFktc4QLM [09:10]). He also reports substantial agreement with RAPM and worse agreement with box plus-minus, which he ties to defensive valuation (JjeFktc4QLM [08:09], [08:40]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's explanation is that defensive value comes from presence and deterrence, not countable actions, and the model credits presence (JjeFktc4QLM [05:07], [09:10]). The captions show no independent check of the defensive value (Inference: the same model produced both the ranking and the 45% figure).

**When to apply** — As a template for checking where a model and a box-score metric disagree: decompose the player's value by source, then ask whether the disagreement lies where the simple metric is blind. Inference: in football, where PFF defensive grades and counting stats diverge for a defender, use film to see whether the gap is coverage or pressure value the counting stats miss.

**When NOT to apply** — A single player, one model, one season of ranking, with no uncertainty shown, so confidence is untested. The 45% and the 54th-versus-12th figures are as spoken and could not be checked against a chart in the captions. Do not treat one disagreement as evidence that defensive specialists are broadly undervalued in markets; the speaker states that as his view (JjeFktc4QLM [09:40]) and the talk shows no market test. # Adding the model improves game prediction over traditional metrics, but the Vegas line stays best

**What it is** — The speaker, Ben Jenkins, tests how well the model predicts games on out-of-sample data, against a Vegas line benchmark. He reports that the Vegas line alone "is obviously the best, has the highest win prediction"; adding the deep RL Shapley values improves over the traditional metrics, and adding the synergy effects improves accuracy further, getting closer to the Vegas line (JjeFktc4QLM [11:42], [12:12]). He concludes the learned values "capture real forward-looking predictive signals" (JjeFktc4QLM [12:12]). The accuracy figures are shown only on a chart and are not stated in the captions, so no effect size can be cited here (JjeFktc4QLM [11:42]). The validation sums the players' Shapley values on the court to predict games, which a judge questioned (JjeFktc4QLM [13:13], [13:44]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond the value being learned from outcomes and including interaction. Inference: a benchmark that already prices public information (the Vegas line) is a hard test, so falling short of it is the expected result for a player-value model rather than a failure.

**When to apply** — As a model for how to validate a player-value metric: hold out data, compare against an existing predictive benchmark, and add the new metric to it rather than replacing it. Inference: a football grade or load metric could be tested the same way against a simple baseline on held-out games.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is supported only for the design: out-of-sample comparison against named benchmarks is reported, but no numbers, no uncertainty, no data split and no number of games appear in the captions. The data are about five seasons of NBA play-by-play (JjeFktc4QLM [16:21]). Do not read this as beating the market: the Vegas line was best (JjeFktc4QLM [11:42]). Do not assume a similar gain for a football metric.

**Example** — The speaker's own ladder: Vegas line alone, then adding the model's values, then adding synergy, each step closer to the Vegas line (JjeFktc4QLM [11:42], [12:12]).
